**Editor's Note:** Academy Award-winning actress Reese Witherspoon serves as the Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation and global ambassador for Avon Products. Here, she speaks out to dispel the persistent myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. 

**(CNN) —** Every three minutes in the United States, another woman receives a breast cancer diagnosis. As a woman, mother, and daughter, I find that statistic profoundly alarming. While I was never naïve about the reality of this disease, understanding the sheer frequency of it brought the issue into sharp, sobering focus. 

Women close to me have fought breast cancer and now stand as brave advocates in the broader crusade against it. Yet the realization of that "every three minutes" benchmark left me feeling deeply vulnerable—a stark reminder that no one is immune. I knew the only way to transform my anxiety into hope was through action. I needed to educate myself and empower others. 

In my role as Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation, I was fortunate to have extraordinary resources at my disposal—an entire organization devoted to uplifting and educating women. Driven by a desire to learn, I asked a simple question: "What do I need to know?" That inquiry led me to the single most critical truth in the fight against breast cancer: **early detection saves lives.** 

According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, when breast cancer is detected before it spreads to other parts of the body, the five-year survival rate rises to 97 percent. Because early-stage breast cancer typically presents no symptoms, regular self-examinations are essential, as is consulting a physician at the first sign of even the subtle changes. 

Discussing breast health is undeniably intimate. As a naturally private person, I understand the hesitation; nevertheless, I urge every woman to set aside her reservations and speak openly with her healthcare providers. We must also dismantle the dangerous myth that youth offers immunity. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met courageous young survivors who were diagnosed in their twenties—a milestone age when most women are graduating from college and embarking on adulthood. 

[*Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »*]

To stay vigilant, women in their 20s and 30s should receive a clinical breast exam by a health professional at least once every three years, while women aged 40 and older should undergo an exam annually. 

My commitment to confronting this devastating disease is deeply personal. I fight for my mother, for myself, for my children, and for future generations, envisioning a day when no woman has to live in fear of breast cancer. My journey began by learning the essential first steps of detection, and it will not end until women everywhere can stand united in declaring a breast-cancer-free world. 

Above all, I hold an unyielding faith that we will find a cure. I saw this shared resolve reflected in the faces of those at the Washington event—the determined walkers, and the crowd of men and women standing along the sidelines, passionately encouraging all 3,500 participants to the finish line. I was right there cheering alongside them, calling for urgent action. 

Avon’s next walk will take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.

The wall clock in the office chimed eight times, but Reese’s desk remained buried under a mountain of paper. As senior editor at *Vanguard Publishing*, her days—and often her nights—were measured in red ink, marginalia, and tight deadlines. She spent her life tucked away in the shadows of storytelling, sculpting raw, unpolished manuscripts into literary gems. 

She reached for the final submission in the stack, ready to call it a night, when something fell out from between the pages. It was a small, pale-blue note, folded in half.

Curious, Reese unfolded it. Written in sharp, elegant cursive was a message meant specifically for her:

*Reese—You spend all your days repairing the architecture of other people’s dreams. It’s time to rebuild your own. Turn to Chapter Four.*

She frowned, looking around the quiet, empty office. Anonymous submissions rarely addressed the editor by name. She flipped through the crisp pages until she reached the specified chapter. The prose was vivid, raw, and painfully familiar. It told the story of a young writer who had set aside her own manuscript years ago to take a job at a prestigious publishing house, trading her creative spark for the safety of a steady paycheck.

It was her own story. 

Tucked into the final margin of the chapter was one last handwritten note: *The red pen can fix mistakes, but it can’t write the future. The ending is yours to finish.*

Reese leaned back in her chair, the weight of the words washing over her. She recognized the handwriting now—it belonged to Julian, the retired editor-in-chief who had hired her years ago and always believed in her talent. He had quietly tracked down her old, discarded draft and placed it right where he knew she couldn't ignore it.

Slowly, Reese set down her red editing pen. She capped it, pulled a fresh sheet of paper from her drawer, and picked up a black fountain pen instead. For the first time in ten years, the editor began to write.

**Title:** The Power of Knowing: Why Early Detection Is Every Woman’s Greatest Defense

**By Reese Witherspoon**

If my career in storytelling has taught me anything, it’s that every woman carries an extraordinary narrative inside her. We are mothers, daughters, entrepreneurs, caregivers, and friends. We juggle a million roles, often placing the needs of everyone else—our children, our partners, our careers—at the very top of our daily to-do lists. 

But too often, we leave our own health at the very bottom. 

Several years ago, I had the incredible honor of serving as the Global Ambassador and Honorary Chairman of the Avon Foundation for Women. When I first stepped into that role, I knew I was joining a legacy of female empowerment. What I didn’t fully grasp until I began traveling the world—meeting women from Tokyo to São Paulo, and right here in the United States—was just how universal our health struggles are, and how profoundly a single diagnosis can ripple through an entire community. 

I will never forget sitting in a small clinic with a group of women who had survived breast cancer. They came from vastly different backgrounds, but they shared a common bond of fierce resilience. Over and over, I heard a recurring theme in their stories: *“I almost didn’t go to my appointment.”* They were too busy. They were afraid of what the doctor might find. They didn't think it could happen to them. 

Yet, for those women, that one routine screening saved their lives. 

The statistics surrounding breast cancer can feel overwhelming. About one in eight women in the U.S. will develop invasive breast cancer over the course of her lifetime. But behind those staggering numbers is a message of immense hope—one that I pledged to amplify during my time with Avon, and one that I continue to champion today: **Early detection saves lives.**

When breast cancer is detected early, in its localized stage, the relative five-year survival rate is nearly 99 percent. Knowledge truly is power. A mammogram isn't just a medical procedure; it is an act of radical self-care. It is taking ownership of your body, your future, and your story. 

Through the Avon Breast Cancer Crusade, I saw firsthand the miraculous impact of getting resources directly to the women who need them most. We worked to fund mobile mammography vans, support cutting-edge research, and bridge the gap for medically underserved communities where access to quality healthcare is a daily hurdle. Breast cancer does not discriminate based on income, race, or geography, and our efforts to fight it shouldn't either. Equity in early detection is a human rights issue. 

However, systemic access is only half the battle. The other half is overcoming the internal barriers—the fear and the delay. 

As women, we have to stop feeling guilty for taking an hour out of our day to see a doctor. We need to normalize talking open-heartedly about our health, performing monthly self-exams, and knowing our family medical histories. We need to create a culture where encouraging your best friend, your sister, or your mother to get her annual mammogram is as routine as calling her to catch up on the weekend. 

If you are reading this right now and you’ve been putting off your annual screening, please consider this your gentle, loving nudge. Pick up the phone. Make the appointment. Talk to your doctor about your risk factors. 

We often talk about sisterhood as a feeling, but at its best, sisterhood is an action. It’s looking out for one another. Through my work with the Avon Foundation, I saw what happens when women unite for a common cause: we move mountains. By prioritizing early detection, taking charge of our health, and lifting as we climb, we can rewrite the narrative around breast cancer—turning fear into action, and diagnoses into stories of survival. 

Your story matters. Your health matters. Take care of yourself today, so you can keep changing the world tomorrow.

# Reese Witherspoon Leads the Charge for Early Detection at Avon Walk for Breast Cancer

**LOS ANGELES** — Standing before a sea of thousands wearing pink ribbons and walking shoes, Oscar-winning actress Reese Witherspoon delivered a passionate message that transcended Hollywood: **early detection saves lives.** 

As the Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation for Women and Avon’s Global Ambassador, Witherspoon took the stage at the Avon Walk for Breast Cancer to urge women everywhere to prioritize their health, schedule regular screenings, and remove the stigma and fear surrounding breast cancer diagnoses.

"Every time we gather for these walks, I am reminded of the immense power of community," Witherspoon told the crowd. "We are here to honor the brave survivors, remember those we’ve lost, and make sure that future generations of women have the tools, knowledge, and resources they need to fight this disease—and win."

### The Power of Early Detection: The Statistics That Matter

During her address, Witherspoon emphasized that while a breast cancer diagnosis is daunting, awareness and early intervention dramatically alter the outcome. She highlighted critical statistics that illustrate why annual mammograms and self-exams are vital.

According to data from the American Cancer Society, when breast cancer is detected early—while it is still localized (confined to the breast)—the **5-year relative survival rate is 99%**. 

"That number—99 percent—is not just a statistic," Witherspoon emphasized. "It represents mothers, daughters, sisters, and friends who get to stay with their families because their cancer was caught early. But when the disease spreads before it is diagnosed, that survival rate drops significantly. That is why waiting is not an option. Early detection is our single best weapon."

Despite these hopeful figures, breast cancer remains the second leading cause of cancer death among women in the United States, with 1 in 8 women expected to develop invasive breast cancer in their lifetime. Witherspoon noted that fear and lack of access to healthcare often prevent women from getting screened early enough.

"So many women put everyone else’s needs before their own," she said. "We take care of our kids, our partners, our jobs, our friends—and we put off our own doctors' appointments. We have to change that mindset. Taking care of yourself is not selfish; it’s essential."

### Walking for a Cure: The Impact of the Avon Walk

The Avon Walk for Breast Cancer, a weekend-long, 39-mile endurance event held in cities across the nation, raises millions of dollars annually to fund biomedical research and ensure access to care. Funds raised directly support vital programs, including providing free mammograms and diagnostic services for uninsured or underinsured women.

Witherspoon praised the participants—many of whom were survivors themselves or walking in memory of loved ones—for their grueling two-day commitment.

"Walking 39 miles over two days takes incredible strength," Witherspoon said. "But the courage shown by the people on this track pales in comparison to the courage it takes to fight cancer. Every step you take, every dollar you raise, brings us closer to a world where no woman has to fear a breast cancer diagnosis."

Through her work with Avon, Witherspoon has traveled internationally to raise awareness not only for breast cancer research but also for global healthcare equity, advocating for women in developing nations who lack basic access to life-saving screenings.

### A Call to Action

Closing her address, Witherspoon issued a direct call to action for everyone in attendance and watching at home.

"I want every woman listening today to do two things," Witherspoon urged. "First, schedule your annual mammogram or screening today if you’re due. Don’t wait. Second, talk to the women in your life—your friends, your sisters, your coworkers—and make sure they are doing the same. Knowledge is power, and action saves lives."

As the walk kicked off, Witherspoon joined participants at the starting line, cheering on the sea of pink as they set off on their 39-mile journey—united in hope, strength, and the shared mission to end breast cancer once and for all.

*** 

### Key Takeaways & Breast Cancer Early Detection Stats:
* **Localized Stage:** If breast cancer is caught before it spreads outside the breast, the 5-year survival rate is **99%**.
* **Regional Stage:** If the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, the 5-year survival rate is approximately **86%**.
* **Distant Stage:** If the cancer has metastasized to distant parts of the body, the 5-year survival rate drops to **30%**.
* **Screening Guidelines:** Women aged 40 and older are encouraged to discuss starting annual mammogram screenings with their healthcare providers.

**By Reese Witherspoon**

***Editor’s Note:** Reese Witherspoon is an Academy Award-winning actress, producer, and entrepreneur. **(CNN) —** Throughout my career, I’ve had the privilege of portraying strong, resilient women on screen. But the most courageous women I have ever met aren’t characters in a script. They are the millions of women worldwide who face a breast cancer diagnosis with fierce determination, and the mothers, sisters, daughters, and friends who stand fiercely by their side.

Every single minute, a woman somewhere in the world dies from breast cancer. That is not just a statistic; it is a heartbreaking loss of stories unfinished, dreams unfulfilled, and families forever changed. Yet, amid this stark reality lies a profound truth that we must repeat until every woman hears it: early detection saves lives. 

When we catch breast cancer in its earliest stages, the odds are overwhelmingly in our favor. The power to rewrite the narrative around this disease often begins with a simple, proactive conversation—one we must encourage every woman in our lives to have.

Too often, young women believe that breast cancer is a disease reserved for later in life. We tend to view ourselves as invincible in our twenties and thirties, balancing careers, families, and endless to-do lists while placing our own health at the very bottom of the priority sheet. But breast cancer does not discriminate by age. 

My message to young women everywhere is simple: get to know your body now. Don’t wait until a routine mammogram at age 40 to pay attention. Learn what is normal for you, ask your relatives about your family’s medical history, and never hesitate to speak up if something feels wrong. You are your own best advocate, and trusting your intuition can literally save your life. 

Taking control of our health isn't just personal—it's a collective effort. That is why my work with Avon and the Avon Foundation for Women has meant so much to me over the years. I have seen firsthand what happens when communities unite around a shared purpose. When we lace up our sneakers for an Avon Walk for Breast Cancer, we aren't just walking miles; we are funding vital medical research, expanding access to care for underserved communities, and ensuring that no woman has to walk through a diagnosis alone.

As we look ahead to the upcoming Avon Walk events across the country, I am reminded that real progress happens step by step, person by person. Whether you are walking in memory of a loved one, celebrating your own survival, or simply showing up for the women you care about, your presence matters.

We have the knowledge, the technology, and the power to change the trajectory of this disease. But awareness only works if it leads to action. 

So today, I ask you to do two things. First, pick up the phone and remind a woman you love—your mother, your sister, your best friend—to schedule her screening or perform a self-check. Second, look into your local community and see how you can get involved, whether by joining an Avon Walk or supporting critical health programs.

We cannot erase breast cancer overnight, but together, through early detection, open conversations, and unwavering solidarity, we can give millions of women the long, healthy futures they deserve.

**Title:** The Myth of Invincibility: Why Young Women Cannot Afford to Ignore Breast Cancer

**By [Name]**  
*Actor, Advocate, and Founder of the Body First Initiative*

When you spend your life in front of a camera, you quickly learn the power of perception. Filters, lighting, and wardrobe can construct an illusion of perfection—and more dangerous still, an illusion of invincibility. For a long time, I believed that my youth was my own personal armor. I believed, as millions of young women do, that serious illness was a distant problem reserved for a much later chapter of life. 

We are taught to worry about our careers, our relationships, our skin routines, and our credit scores. We are not taught to worry about mammograms. 

There is a pervasive, deadly myth whispering to a whole generation of women: *You are too young for breast cancer.* 

I am writing this today to tell you, with absolute urgency, that this myth is killing us. 

Every year, thousands of women under the age of 40 are diagnosed with breast cancer. In fact, breast cancer is the most common cancer in women aged 15 to 39. Yet, because of the lingering misconception that this is an "older woman's disease," young women are routinely left out of the conversation. 

The consequences of this blind spot are devastating. Because routine screening mammograms generally do not begin until age 40, breast cancer in younger women is rarely caught by routine checks. Instead, it is found by the women themselves. And because young women are repeatedly told they aren't at risk, they often wait—months, sometimes—before getting a suspicious lump checked out. Even worse, when they do visit a doctor, their concerns are too frequently brushed off with a reassuring, "You’re too young to worry."

By the time a diagnosis is finally made, the cancer in younger women is often at a later stage and tends to be more aggressive. Triple-negative breast cancer, for instance, occurs at a higher rate in younger, particularly Black and Hispanic, women. 

This isn't just about statistics; it is about human lives. I have held the hands of women in their twenties who had to put their college degrees, their rising careers, and their dreams of starting a family on hold to undergo grueling chemotherapy. I have listened to 30-year-olds navigate early menopause and fertility preservation while fighting for their lives. 

We cannot allow the myth of youth to shield us from reality any longer. It is time to redefine what taking care of ourselves looks like. 

First, we must become the undisputed experts of our own bodies. "Breast self-awareness" shouldn't be a taboo phrase. Know what your breasts normally look and feel like. Lumps aren't the only warning sign—look out for changes in skin texture, dimpling, nipple inversion, or unusual discharge. If you notice a change, do not wait. Do not let fear freeze you, and do not let a busy schedule distract you. 

Second, we must learn our family histories. Genetics play a massive role in early-onset breast cancer. If breast or ovarian cancer runs in your family, talk to a doctor about genetic counseling and early screening protocols. Knowledge is not something to be feared; it is your ultimate leverage.

Finally, we must become relentless self-advocates. If you feel something isn't right, and a doctor tells you that you are "too young" to worry, demand a second opinion. Demand an ultrasound. You know your body better than anyone else, and your age should never be used as a reason to dismiss your pain or concerns. 

I know how easy it is to feel invincible when you are young. I know how tempting it is to scroll past articles like this, assuming they apply to someone else. But cancer does not check your birth certificate. It does not wait until it is convenient. 

We have the power to change the narrative, but only if we shatter the silence. Share this with your sisters, your daughters, your friends, and your colleagues. Let us use our collective voice to replace ignorance with action, and fear with empowerment. 

Your youth is a gift—do not let a myth take it away from you. Touch your breasts, know your risk, and advocate for your life.

Hi friends,

October has always been a special time of year for me. Beyond the crisp fall air and sweater weather, October brings a sea of pink ribbons—a beautiful, powerful reminder of a cause that has been close to my heart for many years: Breast Cancer Awareness Month. 

When I had the incredible privilege of serving as the Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation for Women, I traveled around the globe and met extraordinary women from every walk of life. I sat in living rooms and clinic waiting rooms with survivors, listened to women courageously sharing their diagnosis stories, and saw firsthand the dedicated doctors and advocates fighting on the front lines. 

That experience changed me deeply. It showed me that breast cancer isn't just a medical issue; it's a human story that impacts mothers, daughters, sisters, best friends, and entire communities. But more than anything, my time with the Avon Foundation taught me the profound power of women looking out for other women. 

My personal motivation in this fight comes down to a very simple belief: knowledge is our greatest superpower, and no woman should ever have to face this journey alone or without information. We spend so much of our lives taking care of everyone else—our children, our partners, our friends, our careers. But this month, I want to gently remind you to put *yourself* at the top of your to-do list. 

Early detection saves lives. It really is that simple. So, as we honor the brave survivors, support those currently in treatment, and remember the precious lives we’ve lost, here are a few practical, life-saving steps I encourage every woman to take:

*   **Schedule Your Mammogram:** If you are 40 or older—or younger with a family history—please call your doctor and get that annual screening on the calendar. Don’t procrastinate. 
*   **Know Your "Normal":** Get familiar with your own body through regular self-exams. When you know what’s normal for you, you’re much more likely to notice if something feels different or off.
*   **Uncover Your Family History:** Have an open, honest conversation with your family about health history. Knowing if breast or ovarian cancer runs in your family gives you and your doctor crucial insights to tailor your care.
*   **Be Your Own Advocate:** You know your body better than anyone else. If something doesn't feel right, speak up, ask questions, and keep pushing until you get answers. Never hesitate to seek a second opinion.

This October, let’s make a pact to turn awareness into action. Send a text right now to three women you love—your mom, your sister, your best friend—and ask them if they’ve scheduled their annual check-up. 

When we show up for ourselves and for each other, we are unstoppable. Let’s keep spreading light, love, and life-saving information until breast cancer is a thing of the past.

Sending you all so much love,

**Reese Witherspoon**
